title: Modi Congratulates Vance on New Son as Leaders Review India-US Strategic Ties
excerpt: The phone call covered trade, defense, and technology cooperation, with Modi extending personal congratulations on the birth of Alec Neel Vance — the first baby born to a sitting VP in 150 years.
body:
• PM Modi and US Vice President JD Vance held a phone call on August 8, reviewing progress on trade, defense, critical technologies, energy security, and critical minerals.
  • Modi congratulated Vance and Second Lady Usha Vance on the birth of their fourth child, Alec Neel Vance, born July 19 — the first baby born to a sitting VP in over 150 years.
  • The call reaffirmed sustained momentum in high-level engagements under the India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership.
  • The conversation comes as India and the US move closer to finalizing a Bilateral Trade Agreement, with an Indian parliamentary panel urging swift conclusion of the deal.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with US Vice President JD Vance by phone on Friday, reviewing progress across multiple pillars of the India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership and congratulating the Vance family on the birth of their son.

The two leaders "noted the sustained momentum in the high-level engagements and reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening cooperation in trade, defence, critical and emerging technologies, energy security and critical minerals," according to a statement from the Prime Minister's office.

The Personal Touch

Modi warmly congratulated Vance and Second Lady Usha Vance on the birth of their fourth child, Alec Neel Vance, who was born on July 19 at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center. The baby made history as the first child born to a sitting vice president in more than 150 years.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=KiXkvbSH9tU

Usha Vance, the daughter of Indian immigrants, has become a visible bridge between the two nations. The couple's children — Ewan, 9, Vivek, 6, Mirabel, 4, and now Alec — have personal ties to India through their mother's heritage.

"Received a phone call from US Vice President JD Vance. We discussed ways to further deepen India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership across key areas."

— Narendra Modi, on X, August 8, 2026

Trade Deal Inches Closer

The call comes at a pivotal moment for India-US economic ties. An Indian parliamentary panel on August 6 urged the government to quickly conclude the proposed Bilateral Trade Agreement with the United States, recommending it cover sectors including generic medicines, critical minerals, smartphones, engineering goods, auto components, textiles, and marine products, according to Reuters.

US and Indian officials have said the agreement could be signed within months. The terms of reference for negotiations were finalized during Vance's four-day visit to India in April 2025, when he and Modi launched the India-US COMPACT initiative — Catalyzing Opportunities for Military Partnership, Accelerated Commerce and Technology.

The two sides have set an ambitious target of more than doubling bilateral trade to $500 billion by 2030.

Defense and Technology Ties Deepen

Beyond trade, the leaders discussed cooperation on defense and strategic technologies. India and the US expanded their defense and civil nuclear ties earlier this year, and Modi's February 2025 visit to Washington laid the roadmap for closer cooperation aligned with India's Viksit Bharat 2047 vision and the Trump administration's priorities.

The phone call also covered regional and global developments of mutual interest, though specific topics were not disclosed.

What It Means for the Diaspora

The Modi-Vance relationship carries particular significance for Indian Americans. Usha Vance's Indian heritage and the family's visits to Indian temples and cultural sites have given the bilateral relationship a personal dimension that resonates beyond diplomatic corridors. The trade deal, if concluded, could affect sectors that employ significant numbers of Indian Americans and impact visa and work-permit policies that are central to the diaspora's concerns.
